fixes.explanation: That's right, friend. “But Jonathan did not tell his father.” (1 Samuel 14:1) Jonathan, Saul's son, takes his armor-bearer and goes. Saul is Israel's king, and he's staying under the pomegranate tree in Migron.

Six hundred is right. The troops who were with Saul numbered about six hundred men, and Saul himself was staying under the pomegranate tree in Migron. That's a small crowd for a king. I've seen bigger crowds at a half-price cookie sale.
That number is too big for this spot. The text says the troops with Saul at Migron numbered about six hundred men. Saul is the king of Israel, and he was staying under the pomegranate tree there.
Yes, friend. “But the troops did not know that Jonathan had left.” (1 Samuel 14:3) Saul has about six hundred men with him, and Ahijah the priest is among them. The troops were in the dark about it.
The text says it the other way. “But the troops did not know that Jonathan had left.” (1 Samuel 14:3) Jonathan was gone, and the troops didn't know it. About six hundred men were with Saul.

The text doesn't mention any rivers, friend. It says there were cliffs on both sides of the pass, one named Bozez and the other Seneh. One cliff stood to the north toward Michmash, and the other to the south toward Geba. Jonathan has a pass between two cliffs ahead of him.

The text doesn't mention towers. It says cliffs stood on both sides of the pass, one named Bozez and the other Seneh. Jonathan has a pass between two cliffs to cross. Whatever happens next starts there.

That's Jonathan's whole case. He says, “Nothing can hinder the LORD from saving, whether by many or by few.” Two men against an outpost is a small number. I think he's counting on who the LORD is, not on how many men he has.

Jonathan says the opposite. “Nothing can hinder the LORD from saving, whether by many or by few.” He's heading toward an outpost with exactly one other man, his armor-bearer. That's about as few as it gets.
Nobody sends them home, friend. The men of the outpost call out, “Come on up, and we will teach you a lesson!” They're inviting Jonathan up, not telling him to go back.

That's what the text says. “And the Philistines fell before Jonathan, and his armor-bearer followed and finished them off.” (1 Samuel 14:13) Jonathan climbed up on his hands and feet, with his armor-bearer behind him. The men who promised a lesson are the ones who fell.

That would've been the scary version. The text says, “…the Philistines fell before Jonathan, and his armor-bearer followed and finished them off.” The Philistines fall, and the armor-bearer follows behind to finish them off.

The text says the ground shakes too. “Indeed, the earth quaked, and panic spread from God.” (1 Samuel 14:15) The Philistines are trembling, and so is the earth under them. That verse puts the quake right in the middle of the panic.

Jonathan and his armor-bearer did strike down about twenty men, but the text gives the panic a different source. It says, “…panic spread from God.” (1 Samuel 14:15) That first assault was about twenty men, and the panic reached the camp, the field and all the people.

Yes. While Saul is talking to the priest, “…the commotion in the Philistine camp continued to increase.” Things keep building over there while Saul is talking. Then Saul tells the priest, “Withdraw your hand.”

It goes the other direction, friend. The text says, “…the commotion in the Philistine camp continued to increase.” The Philistines aren't settling down. Then Saul tells the priest, “Withdraw your hand.”

That's what they find. Saul and all his troops march to the battle, “…and they found the Philistines in total confusion, with each man wielding the sword against his neighbor.” (1 Samuel 14:20) That's a heavy scene, friend. The Philistines are in confusion, and the swords are turned on their own.
The camp isn't empty. The text says Saul's troops “…found the Philistines in total confusion…” The Philistines are there, each man wielding the sword against his neighbor.
That's not what the text says, friend. Saul's troops “…found the Philistines in total confusion…” Each man is wielding the sword against his neighbor.

Right, friend. The Hebrews who had gone up to join the Philistines “…now went over to the Israelites who were with Saul and Jonathan.” (1 Samuel 14:21) They had been on the Philistine side, and now they switch. The Israelite side keeps growing.

Yes. The Israelites hiding in the hill country of Ephraim heard that the Philistines were fleeing, and “…they also joined the battle in close pursuit.” (1 Samuel 14:22) They had been hiding, and now they're in the fight. That's quite a change.

They join the pursuit, friend. When they hear the Philistines are fleeing, “…they also joined the battle in close pursuit.” (1 Samuel 14:22) Hiding is where they had been, and the chase is where they join in.

The text names someone else. “So the LORD saved Israel that day…” (1 Samuel 14:23) Saul had about six hundred men with him at the start, and the first strike came from two. The one named as the saver is the LORD.

The text gives the credit somewhere else. “So the LORD saved Israel that day…” (1 Samuel 14:23) Saul is the king, and the story finds him staying under the pomegranate tree at Migron. The one named as the saver is the LORD.
